topics.topic: Owner, record type, and identity for startup probe cleanup failure records
questions: When cleanup of the start probe cannot be confirmed, which module writes the required execution record, and what record type and identity does it use when there is no run element or trial case?

When `sandbox.probe_sandbox` cannot confirm cleanup during start, which module writes which execution record before the start stops, given that neither `runs` nor `functions` called the probe and the probe has no named NodeExecution or TrialExecution?

When cleanup is unconfirmed during `sandbox.probe_sandbox`, which module writes the execution record required by A03 rule 7, and what record type does it write, given that neither `runs` nor `functions` called the execution?

quotes: `module:sandbox`. Check at start that bubblewrap is present and one probe execution succeeds.

probe_sandbox: [VALIDATION_ERROR] MUST raise SandboxUnavailableError naming what is missing when the bubblewrap executable, bwrap, cannot be found on the process's PATH, when bwrap --version, which prints "bubblewrap" and the version, names a version other than the imported RELEASE_BWRAP_VERSION constant, when the resolved interpreter path os.path.realpath(sys.executable) lies under no path of the imported SANDBOX_RUNTIME_PATHS constant, when that interpreter, the one execute_function starts inside bubblewrap, run once through bwrap with the same read-only bindings of the imported SANDBOX_RUNTIME_PATHS constant and the same links of the imported SANDBOX_ROOT_SYMLINKS constant to print platform.python_implementation() and platform.python_version() joined by one space, does not print exactly the imported RELEASE_SANDBOX_INTERPRETER constant, or when one probe execution through execute_function of a minimal implementation with no ports, under bounds equal to the imported RELEASE_CEILING_WALL_TIME_MS, RELEASE_CEILING_MEMORY_BYTES, RELEASE_CEILING_OUTPUT_BYTES and RELEASE_CEILING_PROCESS_COUNT constants, does not end succeeded, naming its outcome.

topics.topic: Required behavior when the cleanup-failure execution record cannot be stored
questions: What must happen if the store call that should write the `crashed`/`cleanup_failed` NodeExecution or TrialExecution fails, given that the kernel must stop but recovery must not execute the element again?
What must happen if the store call that should record `crashed` with `cleanup_failed` itself fails, so the required record cannot come first?

What must happen if the store call that should record `crashed` with `cleanup_failed` fails: must the kernel keep trying until the record is durable, stop without it and permit recovery to execute the element again, or use another durable mechanism?

quotes:
A03 rule 7 records the execution `crashed` with
  `cleanup_failed` and then stops the kernel; the record comes first, so that
  start-up recovery finds the element concluded and never executes it again.

On start, before the surface accepts a request, the kernel turns every
   `in_flight` EffectAttempt into `unknown` (A11 rule 4) and then derives every
   run that has not ended — `running`, `awaiting_approval` or `pending` — again
   from its records, oldest first in store order, rewriting a stored status or
   waiting point that lags them (a decided approval, a resolved attempt, an
   outcome whose run change was lost), and advances, as the
   kernel actor, every run that derivation leaves `running`: a
   function element without a
   concluded record is executed again, which is safe because it has no effect; a `read`
   element without one is sent again; an operation element of another class with
   neither a concluded record nor an EffectAttempt was never sent and is advanced
   as if reached for the first time — an approved, unused approval covers it
   only while the rebuilt request has its `request_digest` (A10 rules 1 and 7).
judgement.why: The unconditional claim that recovery never repeats the element conflicts with the recovery rule that repeats a function element whenever the required concluding store call failed.

witness.initial: A run is `running`, a function element has finished with unconfirmed cleanup, and its concluding NodeExecution has not yet been stored.
events: `runs` calls the store to write the concluding NodeExecution, but the store call fails.
On the next start, `runs` recovers the still-running run from its records.
outcomes: The record must come first, so recovery finds the element concluded and never executes it again.
The failed call leaves no concluded record, so recovery executes the function element again.
witness.observer: The owner reading the recovered run's trace and subsequent status.
basis:
`sandbox` reports that outcome with `SandboxResult.stop_required` true and stops nothing. The module that called
  `sandbox.execute_function` writes the execution's record in its usual store
  call — `runs` the NodeExecution, `functions` the TrialExecution — then does
  nothing more in that request: no further element, no further case, no
  verdict, no activation, no run status.

A call that fails writes and changes no record; the only
   trace it can leave is a published file no record names, which nothing reads:
   a spooled file is replaced at its position, value bytes are reused by equal
   bytes until the next start removes them (rule 4).

`surface` owns it: every failure it
  answers `internal_error` — a store failure, an unconfirmed cleanup, any
  unexpected exception — is answered first, and then `surface.serve_kernel`
  ends the process with a non-zero status, so the next start derives every
  run (A14 rules 5 and 7).

topics.topic: Ownership of SandboxResult and propagation contract for stop_required
questions: Which module owns and defines `SandboxResult`, and through what explicit return contracts do `functions` and `runs` propagate `stop_required` to `surface` after recording the execution, without treating an ordinary `crashed` execution as a process-stop request?

quotes:
`StopRequiredError` is owned by `sandbox`; `SandboxResult` decides
  `stop_required`, and the module that wrote the execution's record raises it
  without reinterpreting the detail code (State 3, "Unconfirmed cleanup").

judge_execution: [RETURN_SHAPE] Returns SandboxResult with the outcome, outputs only for succeeded as PortPayload entries in output port name order (a value as a JsonPayload of its canonical JSON bytes, a file as a FilePayload of its bytes, a many file port as a FileListPayload whose contents are the tuple of its files' bytes in list order), resources_used with elapsed wall_time_ms, peak memory_bytes and the output count as output_bytes, failure_detail, detail_code None except for cleanup_failed, and stop_required true exactly for cleanup_failed and false otherwise.

execute_trial_case: [VALIDATION_ERROR] When the SandboxResult reports stop_required, the execution is recorded first with its crashed outcome and detail_code, and then StopRequiredError is raised so that nothing further runs in the request; this capability does not infer stop from detail_code.

advance_run: [VALIDATION_ERROR] When a function element's outcome is crashed with detail cleanup_failed MUST write that one execution in a RecordRunProgressChange with status running and the waiting points unchanged, execute and reach nothing more, write no other status, and raise StopRequiredError.
judgement.why: The later contracts define the sandbox-owned stop signal, make it true only for cleanup failure, and specify how functions and runs record first and propagate StopRequiredError to surface.

topics.topic: Process termination boundary when the internal-error response cannot be delivered
questions: Does `surface` end the process after one attempt to send the `internal_error`, only after confirmed delivery, or by some other boundary when the client disconnects or response transmission fails?

quotes: serve_kernel: [BEHAVIOR] MUST read at most one byte more of a request body than the imported RELEASE_CEILING_SURFACE_REQUEST_BYTES_MAX constant allows, so an oversized request still reaches answer_request and is refused there; when answer_request raises StopRequiredError or any other failure it let propagate because its answer is internal_error, MUST first send and flush that request's internal_error answer built by translate_failure, without detail, mark the outer serving loop to stop, and return from the handler. serve_kernel processes exactly one request per handle_request call and checks that mark before accepting another; it MUST NOT call HTTPServer.shutdown from the request-handling thread. It then closes the entrance and returns a non-zero exit code, so the next start derives every run that has not ended (A03 rule 7, A14 rules 5 and 7).

The serving owner sends and flushes an internal-error response, marks its
    outer one-request-at-a-time loop to stop, returns from the handler and exits
    non-zero; it never invokes `HTTPServer.shutdown` from that handler.
judgement.why: The later notes choose the local send-and-flush boundary, after which the serving loop is marked to stop, the entrance closes, and the process exits non-zero.
